# Cryptic exons from junction counts {#sec-cryptic}

A **cryptic exon** is a piece of intron that is normally not part of mature
mRNA but gets spliced in under some condition, here the loss of TDP-43
[@ling2015]. Because cryptic exons are, by definition, absent from the
annotation, gene-level counts cannot see them, and annotation-based splicing
tools may miss them too.

What every spliced read *does* leave behind is a **splice junction**: the
exact intron it skipped. recount3 provides junction counts for every sample,
so we can look for cryptic exons without touching a single read. The logic
is simple:

> A cryptic splice junction is **absent from the reference annotation**,
> **absent or very rare in controls**, and **present in the knockdown**.

The hard part is making "absent", "rare" and "present" precise, and doing
so before looking at the answer.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
source("R/helpers.R")
source("R/sashimi.R")
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(GenomicFeatures)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(ggplot2)
})
```
:::


## Junction counts in recount3


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rj <- load_jxn_rse()
samples <- sample_table(rj)
keep_s <- samples$run[samples$sirna %in% c("scramble", "TDP43")]
rj <- rj[, keep_s]
grp <- droplevels(samples[keep_s, "sirna"])
table(grp)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> grp
#> scramble    TDP43 
#>        6        6
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
rj
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> class: RangedSummarizedExperiment 
#> dim: 599768 12 
#> metadata(9): time_created recount3_version ... jxn_format recount3_url
#> assays(1): counts
#> rownames(599768): chr1:11390-12009:+ chr1:11672-12009:+ ...
#>   chrY:26621896-26622511:- chrY:26647510-26650382:+
#> rowData names(6): length annotated ... left_annotated right_annotated
#> colnames(12): SRR8083865 SRR8083866 ... SRR8083880 SRR8083881
#> colData names(175): rail_id external_id ...
#>   recount_pred.curated.cell_line BigWigURL
```


:::
:::


Each row is one junction, written as `chrom:start-end:strand`, where
`start` and `end` are the **first and last base of the intron** (1-based,
inclusive). The strand is inferred from the splice-site motif (GT-AG and its
variants), not from the library, which is why it is available even for this
unstranded data set. A few hundred junctions have an unknown strand
(non-canonical motifs); we drop them, together with junctions that have no
reads in our 12 samples.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
jr <- rowRanges(rj)
keep_j <- as.character(strand(jr)) != "*" & rowSums(assay(rj)) > 0
rj <- rj[keep_j, ]
jr <- rowRanges(rj)
cnt <- as.matrix(assay(rj))
kd <- grp == "TDP43"; ct <- grp == "scramble"
c(junctions = nrow(rj), reads = sum(cnt))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> junctions     reads 
#>    521140  93713132
```


:::
:::


## Which junctions are in GENCODE v26?

recount3 adds its own annotation flags, but they are computed against a
*union* of several annotations (GENCODE releases, RefSeq and others). To keep
one annotation throughout, we build the intron list from the same GENCODE v26
GTF that produced our gene counts.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
txdb <- gencode_txdb()
introns <- unique(unlist(intronsByTranscript(txdb)))
length(introns)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 384673
```


:::
:::


Before trusting any overlap, check that the two coordinate systems agree. If
junction and intron coordinates were off by one base, almost nothing would
match exactly:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tot <- rowSums(cnt)
frac_annot <- function(gr) sum(tot[gr %in% introns]) / sum(tot)
round(c(as_is = frac_annot(jr),
        shift_minus1 = frac_annot(shift(jr, -1)),
        shift_plus1  = frac_annot(shift(jr, 1))), 4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>        as_is shift_minus1  shift_plus1 
#>       0.9817       0.0000       0.0000
```


:::
:::


About 98% of all junction reads fall exactly on a GENCODE v26 intron, and
almost none do after a one-base shift, so the conventions match.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Always run a coordinate sanity check
BED files are 0-based and half-open; GTF, SAM and recount3 are 1-based; some
tools report the last exon base instead of the first intron base. A shift of
one base silently turns every annotated junction into a "novel" one. The
check above takes one line and catches that.
:::

Each junction is now classified by its two ends. On the plus strand the
intron start is the 5' splice site (donor) and the end is the 3' splice site
(acceptor); on the minus strand it is the other way round.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
key <- function(chr, pos, str) paste(chr, pos, str)
donor_pos    <- function(gr) ifelse(strand(gr) == "+", start(gr), end(gr))
acceptor_pos <- function(gr) ifelse(strand(gr) == "+", end(gr), start(gr))
known_donor    <- key(seqnames(introns), donor_pos(introns), strand(introns))
known_acceptor <- key(seqnames(introns), acceptor_pos(introns), strand(introns))

annotated <- jr %in% introns
d_ok <- key(seqnames(jr), donor_pos(jr), strand(jr)) %in% known_donor
a_ok <- key(seqnames(jr), acceptor_pos(jr), strand(jr)) %in% known_acceptor
jclass <- case_when(
  annotated     ~ "annotated",
  d_ok & a_ok   ~ "known sites, new pair",
  d_ok & !a_ok  ~ "novel acceptor",
  !d_ok & a_ok  ~ "novel donor",
  TRUE          ~ "both sites novel")
table(jclass)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> jclass
#>             annotated      both sites novel known sites, new pair 
#>                227156                 90465                 52822 
#>        novel acceptor           novel donor 
#>                 81193                 69504
```


:::
:::


How does this compare with recount3's own flag?


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
table(recount3_annotated = jr$annotated, GENCODE_v26 = annotated)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                   GENCODE_v26
#> recount3_annotated  FALSE   TRUE
#>                  0 226597      0
#>                  1  67387 227156
```


:::
:::


Tens of thousands of junctions that recount3 calls "annotated" are not in
GENCODE v26; they come from other annotation sources. Using the recount3 flag
would therefore mix annotations, which is exactly what we want to avoid.

## Junction usage: a PSI for splice sites

Raw junction counts depend on sequencing depth and on how much the gene is
expressed. To compare a junction across samples we use its **usage**: the
fraction of reads at its splice sites that use this particular junction.

$$
\text{usage}_j = \frac{n_j}{\max\left(\sum_{k \in D(j)} n_k,\ \sum_{k \in A(j)} n_k\right)}
$$

where $D(j)$ is the set of junctions that share the donor of $j$ and $A(j)$
the set that share its acceptor. Usage behaves like a percent spliced in
(PSI) for one splice site: 0 means never used, 1 means always used.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sum_by <- function(keys) {
  m <- rowsum(cnt, keys)
  m[match(keys, rownames(m)), , drop = FALSE]
}
den <- pmax(sum_by(key(seqnames(jr), donor_pos(jr), strand(jr))),
            sum_by(key(seqnames(jr), acceptor_pos(jr), strand(jr))))
usage <- cnt / den
usage_kd <- rowMeans(usage[, kd], na.rm = TRUE)
usage_ct <- rowMeans(usage[, ct], na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::


## Two predefined definitions of "cryptic"

There is no single correct way to turn "absent in control, present in
knockdown" into numbers, so we wrote down two definitions **before**
looking at any candidate, and we report both.

Both require that the junction is **not in GENCODE v26** and that it is
**supported in the knockdown**: at least 3 reads in at least 4 of the 6
knockdown samples (a replicate-consistency rule, so that one sample cannot
create a candidate on its own).

| | Definition A: absolute | Definition B: relative |
|---|---|---|
| Control | at most 2 reads in total across the 6 scramble samples | mean usage < 0.05 |
| Knockdown | at least 20 reads in total | mean usage at least 0.1 higher than control |
| Weakness | depends on depth and on gene expression | can miss rare junctions in highly expressed genes |

The 0.1 in definition B is the same effect size as our splicing default
(|ΔPSI| > 0.1).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
novel <- !annotated
support_kd <- rowSums(cnt[, kd] >= 3) >= 4
def_A <- novel & support_kd & rowSums(cnt[, ct]) <= 2 & rowSums(cnt[, kd]) >= 20
def_B <- novel & support_kd & usage_ct < 0.05 & (usage_kd - usage_ct) >= 0.1
c(definition_A = sum(def_A), definition_B = sum(def_B),
  both = sum(def_A & def_B), union = sum(def_A | def_B))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> definition_A definition_B         both        union 
#>           21           29           10           40
```


:::
:::


### Positive control: STMN2

*STMN2* is the best-documented cryptic exon target of TDP-43 in human motor
neurons [@klim2019; @melamed2019]. In the knockdown, exon 1 splices to a
cryptic exon (often called exon 2a) inside intron 1 instead of to exon 2.
Any sensible method should find it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
s2 <- names(jr) == "chr8:79611215-79616821:+"   # exon 1 -> cryptic exon 2a
stmn2 <- which(as.character(seqnames(jr)) == "chr8" & start(jr) == 79611215 &
                 strand(jr) == "+")
data.frame(junction = names(jr)[stmn2], class = jclass[stmn2],
           reads_KD = rowSums(cnt[stmn2, kd, drop = FALSE]),
           reads_control = rowSums(cnt[stmn2, ct, drop = FALSE]),
           usage_KD = round(usage_kd[stmn2], 3), usage_control = round(usage_ct[stmn2], 3),
           def_A = def_A[stmn2], def_B = def_B[stmn2]) |>
  arrange(desc(reads_KD)) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

:::
:::


The junction from exon 1 to the cryptic exon (`chr8:79611215-79616821:+`)
has 4,352 reads in the knockdown, and
on average 28% of exon 1 splicing uses it. Yet
**definition A misses it**, because 21 reads in the
controls are "more than 2". In a highly expressed gene like *STMN2* even a
very rare event (usage 0.001 in controls) produces a
few reads. This is the weakness of absolute thresholds, and the reason
definition B exists. Definition B, in turn, misses rare cryptic junctions in
genes where the normal junction dominates. Reporting both, plus their union,
is more honest than picking whichever looks better.

## The candidate list


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
genes <- genes(txdb, single.strand.genes.only = TRUE)
gtf_genes <- rtracklayer::import(gencode_gtf(), feature.type = "gene")
gene_name <- setNames(gtf_genes$gene_name, gtf_genes$gene_id)
gene_type <- setNames(gtf_genes$gene_type, gtf_genes$gene_id)
name_junction <- function(idx) {
  ov <- findOverlaps(jr[idx], genes, type = "within")
  hits <- data.frame(q = queryHits(ov), id = names(genes)[subjectHits(ov)])
  hits$pc <- gene_type[hits$id] == "protein_coding"
  hits <- hits[order(hits$q, !hits$pc), ]
  out <- rep(NA_character_, length(idx))
  first <- hits[!duplicated(hits$q), ]
  out[first$q] <- gene_name[first$id]
  out
}
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cand_idx <- which(def_A | def_B)
cand <- data.frame(
  junction = names(jr)[cand_idx],
  gene = name_junction(cand_idx),
  class = jclass[cand_idx],
  reads_KD = rowSums(cnt[cand_idx, kd]),
  reads_control = rowSums(cnt[cand_idx, ct]),
  usage_KD = round(usage_kd[cand_idx], 3),
  usage_control = round(usage_ct[cand_idx], 3),
  def_A = def_A[cand_idx], def_B = def_B[cand_idx]
) |>
  mutate(delta_usage = round(usage_KD - usage_control, 3)) |>
  arrange(desc(delta_usage))
write.csv(cand, "results/cryptic_junction_candidates.csv", row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(cand, row.names = FALSE)
```

but a match in the literature is support, not proof. A list like this is a
set of **candidates**: every line still needs to be looked at before it can
be called a cryptic exon.

pd <- data.frame(u_ct = usage_ct, u_kd = usage_kd,

ggplot(arrange(pd, status != "neither"), aes(u_ct, u_kd, colour = status)) +

  geom_point(size = 1.4, alpha = 0.8) +

## From junctions to exons

A cassette cryptic exon leaves **two** novel junctions: one into the exon
(its acceptor is new) and one out of it (its donor is new). On the genome,
the first junction ends just before the exon and the second starts just
after it. We can pair them automatically among all novel junctions with
knockdown support.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sup <- which(novel & support_kd)
s_gr <- jr[sup]
# For every junction i, look for a junction j that starts 1 to 500 bases after
# i ends, on the same chromosome and strand. The bases in between are the exon.
after_i <- GRanges(seqnames(s_gr), IRanges(end(s_gr) + 2, end(s_gr) + 501), strand = strand(s_gr))
start_j <- GRanges(seqnames(s_gr), IRanges(start(s_gr), width = 1), strand = strand(s_gr))
ov <- findOverlaps(after_i, start_j)
cryptic_exons <- data.frame(i = queryHits(ov), j = subjectHits(ov)) |>
  mutate(chrom = as.character(seqnames(s_gr))[i], strand = as.character(strand(s_gr))[i],
         exon_start = end(s_gr)[i] + 1, exon_end = start(s_gr)[j] - 1,
         exon_length = exon_end - exon_start + 1,
         in_junction = names(s_gr)[i], out_junction = names(s_gr)[j]) |>
  filter(in_junction %in% cand$junction | out_junction %in% cand$junction) |>
  mutate(gene = name_junction(sup[i]),
         frame = ifelse(exon_length %% 3 == 0, "in frame (multiple of 3)", "frameshift")) |>
  select(gene, chrom, exon_start, exon_end, strand, exon_length, frame, in_junction, out_junction)
write.csv(cryptic_exons, "results/cryptic_exons_paired.csv", row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(cryptic_exons, row.names = FALSE)
```

Three things in this table deserve a comment:

- The main *STMN2* event (exon 1 to exon 2a) is **not** in the table. The
  cryptic exon 2a has a junction into it but none out of it, because
  transcripts end inside it at a cryptic polyadenylation site
  [@melamed2019]. It behaves like an alternative last exon, not a cassette
  exon. Keep this in mind for @sec-rmats, where we use a tool that models
  cassette-type events. What the table does show for *STMN2* is a minor
  path through a small 115-nt exon between exon 1 and exon 2a; you can see
  its two small arcs in the *STMN2* sashimi plot below.
- Rows without a gene name on chromosome 17 (around 38 Mb) fall in the
  *TBC1D3* gene family, a set of near-identical gene copies created by
  segmental duplication. Reads there can be assigned to the wrong copy, so
  these candidates need extra caution.
- Some pairs share one junction (for example two alternative acceptors in
  *SLC24A3*). Junction pairing describes possible exons; it does not tell
  you which transcript isoforms exist.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Frameshift is not the same as "undergoes NMD"
A cryptic exon whose length is not a multiple of 3 shifts the reading frame
and usually creates a premature termination codon (PTC). If that PTC lies
more than about 50 to 55 nucleotides upstream of the last exon-exon
junction, the transcript is **predicted** to be a target of nonsense-mediated
decay [@nagy1998]. This is a prediction from sequence. Saying that a
transcript "undergoes NMD" requires experiments, for example blocking NMD
(cycloheximide, or knockdown of UPF1) and showing that the cryptic isoform
accumulates.
:::

The two junctions that flank the cryptic exon (`17641557-17642413` and
`17642542-17642844`) are absent from all six controls and present in several
knockdown samples, but with only a handful of reads, so they fail the
support rule (3 reads in at least 4 of 6 knockdown samples). The pattern is
consistent with the published cryptic exon, but it does not pass our
predefined criteria. The correct description is an **exploratory signal**,
not a finding. With a partial knockdown, a cell-type-specific gene and
12 to 57 million read pairs per sample, that is about what one should
expect.

## Visual confirmation

Counts alone are not enough to claim a cryptic exon: a junction can come
from a mapping artefact, a repeat, or a single odd sample. The standard
check is a **sashimi plot**: read coverage along the gene with arcs showing
junction reads. A real cryptic exon shows coverage over the new exon in the
knockdown, together with arcs into (and, for cassette exons, out of) it.

We build a simple sashimi-style plot from recount3 files only: coverage
from the per-sample BigWig files and arcs from the junction counts
(`R/sashimi.R`). For publication-quality plots from BAM files, use ggsashimi
[@garridomartin2018] or IGV [@robinson2011].


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
mapped <- setNames(samples$mapped_pairs, samples$run)
groups <- list(scramble = keep_s[ct], `TDP-43 KD` = keep_s[kd])
gcols <- c(scramble = unname(SIRNA_COLS["scramble"]), `TDP-43 KD` = unname(SIRNA_COLS["TDP43"]))
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sashimi_plot("chr8", 79610500, 79638500, "+", groups, cnt, jr, novel, txdb, mapped,
             min_mean_reads = 5, title = "STMN2", group_cols = gcols)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![STMN2, exon 1 to exon 2. In the knockdown, an unannotated junction (orange arc) leads from exon 1 into intron 1, coverage appears just downstream of it (the cryptic exon 2a), and coverage over exon 2 drops. Group means hide variation between samples. Before you report a cryptic
exon, also look at each sample separately (the per-sample junction counts
in the tables above, or individual BAM files in IGV, as in @sec-rmats).

## What we can and cannot say

| Statement | Supported here? |
|---|---|
| "Knockdown of TDP-43 is associated with inclusion of an unannotated exon in *STMN2*" | Yes: junction counts in all 6 KD samples, near-absent in controls, visible in coverage |
| "The *STMN2* cryptic exon reduces STMN2 protein" | No: RNA-seq does not measure protein |
| "*UNC13A* cryptic exon inclusion" | Exploratory signal only: consistent direction, too few reads to pass our criteria |
| "Cryptic exon X causes NMD" | No: at most "predicted NMD target" from sequence |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding
1. Why do we define "annotated" with our own GENCODE v26 intron list
   instead of the `annotated` column that recount3 provides?
2. Definition A misses the *STMN2* cryptic junction. Should we loosen
   definition A until it is found?
3. A candidate junction has 40 reads in one knockdown sample and 0 in the
   other five. Does it pass the support rule? Should it?
4. Why does the *STMN2* cryptic exon not appear in the paired-junction
   table?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answers
1. The recount3 flag uses a union of annotation sources and releases. Mixing
   it with GENCODE v26 gene counts would break the one-annotation rule and
   change what "novel" means.
2. No. Changing a threshold until a favoured gene appears is tuning to the
   result. The right response is what we did: understand why it is missed
   (an absolute count threshold depends on expression), use a second
   predefined definition that addresses that weakness, and report both.
3. No: the rule needs at least 3 reads in at least 4 of 6 knockdown samples.
   A signal from one sample could be a sample-specific artefact or a
   mapping problem; replication across samples is the point.
4. The cryptic exon is a terminal exon (transcripts end in it), so there is
   a junction into it but none out of it. Our pairing looks for cassette
   exons with junctions on both sides.
:::
:::
